canonicalName: Jaina permutations and combinations (early Indian combinatorics)

milestones.label: Bhagavati Sutra gives counting rules for selections from n
milestones.work: Bhagabati (Bhagavati) Sutra, Jaina canon, undated; MacTutor puts it around 300 BC
milestones.description: The canon states how many permutations and combinations arise when one, two or three items are chosen from n, and works out cases n = 2, 3, 4.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Jaina mathematics: Bhagabati Sutra dated around 300 BC, rules for permutations and combinations of 1, 2, 3 from n
Wikipedia Indian mathematics: Jain texts incl. Sthananga Sutra, c. 300 BCE-200 CE, as the main Jain mathematical sources

milestones.note: Dating of Jaina canonical texts is uncertain and later commentaries are the working evidence; no critical edition/Crossref record for the original text was found, so this stays a history-page claim.

milestones.label: Pingala enumerates metres as binary patterns of short and long syllables
milestones.work: Pingala, Chandahsastra (Chandas Sutra), Sanskrit prosody
milestones.description: Pingala systematically lists and counts all light/heavy syllable patterns of a given length, with a triangular array of binomial counts, using combinatorics on a purposeful target (metre).

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Pingala: Chandahshastra enumerates metres by recursive generation of light/guru patterns, counts via binomial coefficients, meru-prastara triangle; Pingala c. 3rd-2nd century BCE

milestones.note: Date given as c. 3rd or 2nd century BCE; may be parallel to or later than the Jaina canon, so ordering against the Bhagavati Sutra is uncertain. Wikipedia is the only source read; not independently checked against Weber/other editions.

milestones.label: Anuyogadvara Sutra: earliest Indian description of factorials
milestones.work: Anuyogadvara Sutra, Jaina canon, c. 200 BCE-100 CE
milestones.description: The Anuyogadvara Sutra is reported to contain the earliest known Indian description of factorial products, extending counting of arrangements.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Indian mathematics: Anuyogadwara Sutra (c. 200 BCE-100 CE) includes the earliest known description of factorials in Indian mathematics

milestones.note: Single secondary source; date range wide.

milestones.label: Sthananga Sutra lists permutations and combinations among the topics of mathematics
milestones.work: Sthananga (Sthanaanga) Sutra, Jaina canon, about the 2nd century BC
milestones.description: The Sthananga Sutra names permutations and combinations as a standing branch of mathematics and uses them, setting the curriculum for later Indian work.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: Sthananga Sutra from about the 2nd century BC lists topics incl. permutations and combinations; permutations and combinations used in it
MacTutor Indian mathematics: main topics of Jaina mathematics c. 150 BC include permutations and combinations

milestones.label: Mahavira gives special rules for permutations and combinations in a textbook
milestones.work: Mahavira, Ganita Sara Samgraha, c. 850 (Mysore); English edition by M. Rangacarya 1912
milestones.description: Mahavira treats permutations and combinations as a regular topic of a mathematics compendium that updates Brahmagupta, the first systematic textbook treatment found here.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Mahavira: Ganita Sara Samgraha dated 850 AD; he gave special rules for permutations and combinations, a topic of special interest in Jaina mathematics
Open Library records an edition of the Ganita-sara-sangraha with English translation (1912)

milestones.note: MacTutor Zero gives 830 for the same book; 850 is used here as given on his own biography page. I did not read the text itself, so the exact formulas (whether the general n-choose-r rule is stated) are not verified.

works.whyItMatters: earliest known systematic enumeration of syllable patterns, binomial counts
compendium with explicit rules for permutations and combinations

notes: Disputed: relative order of the Jaina canon and Pingala; both are dated only to broad ranges. No naming milestone found: no indigenous term for the field could be dated (searched MacTutor Jaina page, Wikipedia Indian mathematics). Modern scholarship: Kusuba and Plofker, Indian combinatorics (Combinatorics: Ancient and Modern, 2013, doi 10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199656592.003.0002) and Mathematics in Ancient Jaina Literature (2022, doi 10.1142/9789811255502_0005) were found in Crossref but not read. Event summary bundles Jaina cosmology and infinities; those are outside the permutations story. No MSC milestone: 05A has no dated origin for this event.

canonicalName: Diophantus and the Arithmetica (symbolic algebra and Diophantine problems)

milestones.label: Old Babylonian procedures for solving quadratic-type problems
milestones.work: Old Babylonian mathematical tablets (Susa, Nippur, etc.)
milestones.description: Problem-solving that modern historians call algebra already existed in Mesopotamia long before Diophantus, so the Arithmetica is not the start of the technique itself.

evidence.claim: Hoyrup 2002 chapters characterise Old Babylonian "algebra" as a body of procedures
evidence.source: Hoyrup, Old Babylonian Algebra: a global characterization (2002)

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Diophantus: he did not invent the method of algebra, which existed before him

milestones.note: Date is the conventional Old Babylonian range (c. 1800-1600 BCE), not from the cited chapters.

milestones.label: Arithmetica written (13 books, 290 problems)
milestones.work: Diophantus, Arithmetica; Greek, Alexandria; composition date uncertain
milestones.description: Diophantus collects numerical problems solved by equations in one unknown and introduces abbreviations for the unknown, its powers and equality.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Diophantus: wrote after Hypsicles (150 BC) and before Theon of Alexandria (350 AD); symbolism with abbreviations for unknown and powers
Wikipedia Diophantus: flourished c. 250 CE, possible span 170 BCE-350 CE; 290 problems, six books in Greek, four in Arabic

milestones.note: Date is conventional (fl. c. 250 CE). Hard bounds from citations: later than Hypsicles (c. 150-170 BCE), earlier than Theon (350 CE); the range end 350 is the latest bound only. Treat derived conceptual date 250 as a convention.

milestones.label: Regiomontanus announces the Greek Diophantus to Latin Europe
milestones.work: Regiomontanus, remark of 1463 that no one had yet translated the thirteen books
milestones.description: Regiomontanus reports the Greek text and says it is untranslated, reopening Diophantus to European mathematicians.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Diophantus: Europe learnt of the Arithmetica via Regiomontanus in 1463; Bombelli translated much of it in 1570 without publishing

milestones.label: Bachet's Greek-Latin edition of the Arithmetica
milestones.work: Bachet, Diophanti Alexandrini Arithmeticorum libri sex, Paris 1621
milestones.description: Bachet prints the Greek text with a Latin translation and commentary, giving the first widely used scholarly edition.

evidence.claim: Open Library lists the 1621 edition Diophanti Alexandrini Arithmeticorum libri sex
Wikipedia Diophantus: the 1621 Bachet edition gained fame through Fermat marginal Last Theorem note

milestones.note: A critical edition rather than a textbook; used for the consolidation role as the first systematic printed treatment.

milestones.label: Fermat's marginal notes published with Bachet's edition
milestones.work: Diophanti Alexandrini Arithmeticorum libri sex ... cum observationibus P. de Fermat, Toulouse 1670 (ed. Samuel de Fermat)
milestones.description: Samuel Fermat publishes his father's observations on Diophantus, which launch modern Diophantine analysis (e.g. the Last Theorem note).

evidence.claim: MacTutor Fermat: marginal notes became known when Samuel published an edition of Bachet with his father notes in 1670
Open Library lists the 1670 edition with Fermat as contributor

milestones.label: Heath's study of Diophantus in English
milestones.work: T. L. Heath, Diophantus of Alexandria: a study in the history of Greek algebra, Cambridge 1885 (2nd ed. 1910)
milestones.description: Heath provides the standard English monograph and translation, consolidating Diophantus for the modern reader.

evidence.claim: Open Library lists Heath, Diophantus of Alexandria, first published 1885 (also 1910)

milestones.note: Role chosen as a monograph; Nesselmann 1842 or Tannery 1893-95 may precede in scholarly editions (not searched).

milestones.label: Arabic Books IV-VII identified and edited
milestones.work: Sesiano, Books IV to VII of Diophantus Arithmetica in the Arabic translation attributed to Qusta ibn Luqa, Springer 1982
milestones.description: A manuscript found in 1968 preserves four further books in Arabic, changing the picture of what the Arithmetica contained.

evidence.claim: Crossref records Sesiano 1982, Books IV to VII of Diophantus Arithmetica
MacTutor Diophantus: Sezgin found Arabic manuscript of Books IV-VII in 1968; Rashed argued it is a translation by Qusta ibn Luqa (d. 912)

milestones.note: Authenticity as Diophantus text is questioned by some reviewers (Rozenfeld quoted by MacTutor).

works.whyItMatters: problems solved by algebra with symbolic abbreviations

works.citation: Books IV to VII of Diophantus Arithmetica

notes: Disputed: Diophantus date (about 500-year window); whether the symbolism was his own (MacTutor quoting Vogel) or pre-existing (Wikipedia). Methodological date left null: no purposeful application to an outside target was dated. Naming of Diophantine equations/analysis as a field name not dated; searched MacTutor and Wikipedia Diophantus. MSC 11D (Diophantine equations) exists but its first-appearance year was not established. Biographical lifespans of Heath and Sesiano come from memory and are flagged; Bachet lifespan not re-read on the MacTutor page.

canonicalName: Discovery of incommensurable magnitudes (irrationality of the diagonal)
aliases: irrationality of the square root of 2

milestones.label: First proof that side and diagonal of a square are incommensurable (attributed, disputed)
milestones.work: Pythagorean school; attributed to Hippasus of Metapontum; no surviving text
milestones.description: A Pythagorean showed that the diagonal of a square has no common measure with its side, breaking the claim that all magnitudes are ratios of whole numbers.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Hippasus: sometimes credited with discovery of irrationals; no ancient writer ascribes it to him specifically; he lived c. 530 - c. 450 BC
Von Fritz 1945 studies the attribution to Hippasus in the Annals of Mathematics
evidence.source: K. von Fritz, Annals of Mathematics 46 (1945)

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Irrational number: first proof attributed to a Pythagorean, possibly Hippasus, 5th century BC

milestones.note: No text from the period survives; date is a scholarly attribution (5th century BCE). Role first_statement is used for lack of a surviving earlier statement; the earliest surviving evidence is Plato/Aristotle/Euclid.

milestones.label: Theodorus proves irrationality of the roots of 3, 5, ... up to 17
milestones.work: Reported in Plato, Theaetetus (dialogue set in 399 BC)
milestones.description: Theodorus handles non-square numbers case by case, without a general theorem, which prompts the general question taken up by Theaetetus.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Theodorus: Plato describes his proofs for roots of 3, 5, ... 17 and notes that the root of 2 was already known irrational
MacTutor Theaetetus: the conversation in the dialogue took place in 399 BC

milestones.note: Date is the dramatic date of Plato dialogue, not publication; Wikipedia gives Theodorus c. 400 BC.

milestones.label: Theaetetus develops a general theory of irrational lengths
milestones.work: Reconstructed from Euclid, Elements Book X and XIII
milestones.description: Theaetetus classifies incommensurable lengths in general; later Book X of the Elements is believed to describe his work.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Theaetetus: Books X and XIII of the Elements are almost certainly a description of his work; born about 417 BC, died about 369 BC

milestones.note: Dated by his lifespan; no writing survives.

milestones.label: Eudoxus defines equality of ratios, covering irrational magnitudes
milestones.work: Eudoxus; preserved in Euclid, Elements Book V
milestones.description: Eudoxus gives a definition of proportion that treats commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes alike, restoring a foundation for geometry.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Eudoxus: theory of proportion allowing possibly irrational lengths to be compared; lived 408-355 BC
Wikipedia Irrational number: Eudoxus formalised a theory of proportion for commensurable and incommensurable quantities

milestones.note: Dated by lifespan (408-355 BC); no work of Eudoxus survives.

milestones.label: Euclid Elements Book V (proportion) and Book X (irrationals)
milestones.work: Euclid, Elements, Alexandria, c. 300 BC
milestones.description: Euclid sets out the theory of proportion and a classification of irrational lines as parts of one deductive treatise.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Euclid: born about 325 BC; the Elements is his treatise; MacTutor Theaetetus says Book X describes irrational lengths
Fowler 1992 invites reading of Book X of the Elements

milestones.note: Date approximate (c. 300 BC).

works.citation: K. von Fritz, The discovery of incommensurability by Hippasus of Metapontum

works.whyItMatters: irrationality of the roots of 3 to 17

works.citation: Work reflected in Elements Book X

notes: Disputed: attribution to Hippasus (no ancient writer names him for irrationality; Iamblichus ties his drowning to the dodecahedron); which magnitude (pentagon/golden ratio vs square diagonal) came first; whether Knorr rational-diameter reconstruction (Amer. Math. Monthly 1998, doi 10.2307/3109803) is right. Aristotle (Prior Analytics) mentions the odd/even argument for the diagonal but no dated record was read, so no milestone. Methodological date left null: no purposeful application to a target was dated. No naming/institution milestone for pre-MSC era. Knorr, The Evolution of the Euclidean Elements (1975; Open Library OL4313763W) is the standard modern reference, not read.

milestones.label: Sunzi suanjing poses the 3-5-7 remainder problem
milestones.work: Sunzi suanjing (Sun Zi mathematical manual), China, 3rd-5th century
milestones.description: A single puzzle asks for a number with given remainders mod 3, 5 and 7, and gives a procedure for it; this is the earliest known occurrence of the problem type.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Chinese overview: earliest known occurrence of a Chinese remainder type problem, in Sun Zi (about 400-about 460)
MacTutor Sun Zi: dating of the Sunzi suanjing ranges from 3rd to 5th century AD across modern authors
Wikipedia CRT: earliest known statement of the problem in the 5th-century Sunzi Suanjing; it is one case, not a theorem

milestones.note: Date range 3rd-5th c. (precision range 300-500); Shen 1988 (doi 10.1007/bf00357063) is the standard history but was not read. Sunzi gives one instance only.

milestones.label: Aryabhata describes the kuttaka algorithm for indeterminate remainders
milestones.work: Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya, 499
milestones.description: Aryabhata gives a pulverising algorithm (Euclidean-style) for solving remainder problems that arise from planetary periods, a general method beyond a single puzzle.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Aryabhata: Aryabhatiya finished 499; kuttaka method for ax-by=c from planetary period problems, related to Euclidean algorithm
Wikipedia CRT: an algorithm for the problem was described by Aryabhata (6th century)

milestones.note: Kuttaka is for linear indeterminate equations; its identification with the full CRT for several moduli is as stated by Wikipedia and not checked in the Aryabhatiya.

milestones.label: Fibonacci includes remainder problems in Liber Abaci
milestones.work: Fibonacci, Liber Abaci, 1202
milestones.description: Special cases of the remainder problem appear in the first major European arithmetic of the Hindu-Arabic era.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia CRT: special cases appear in Fibonacci Liber Abaci (1202)
Open Library lists Sigler translation of Fibonacci Liber Abaci (2002)

milestones.note: Only secondary; not checked in the translation.

milestones.label: Qin Jiushao: general Dayan rule for systems of congruences, including non-coprime moduli
milestones.work: Qin Jiushao, Shushu jiuzhang (Mathematical treatise in nine sections), 1247
milestones.description: Qin gives a complete, systematic algorithm for simultaneous congruences, opening his treatise with it and treating even rational and non-coprime moduli.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Qin Jiushao: Shushu Jiuzhang appeared in 1247; chapter 1 on indeterminate analysis with the Chinese remainder theorem; problems with rational moduli
Libbrecht studied the treatise (Chinese Mathematics in the Thirteenth Century, 1973)
Shen 1988, Historical development of the Chinese remainder theorem
evidence.source: K. Shen, Arch. Hist. Exact Sci. 38 (1988)

milestones.label: Gauss introduces congruence notation and treats the theorem systematically
milestones.work: C. F. Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, 1801
milestones.description: Gauss gives congruences their notation and theory and solves a calendar-cycle problem with the remainder method, founding the modern treatment.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia CRT: congruences first introduced by Gauss in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae of 1801, illustrated with a calendar problem
Open Library lists Disquisitiones arithmeticae, 1801

milestones.note: Euler used the procedure earlier (Wikipedia); no earlier general treatise located.

notes: Disputed: Sunzi date. Special cases by Brahmagupta (7th c.) are mentioned in Wikipedia; not verified. The name Chinese remainder theorem: coinage and first use not established; searched MacTutor, Wikipedia, Crossref. Wikipedia says Wylie translated Qin in the early 19th century (probably wrong; not checked). Event type import-from-outside: calendar/planetary-period problems motivate Aryabhata and Qin (MacTutor). Methodological date left null: a first purposeful application on a target problem is arguably Aryabhata (planet periods) but is folded into key_development.

canonicalName: Indian sine (jya) and the birth of trigonometric functions

milestones.label: Hipparchus's table of chords
milestones.work: Hipparchus, chord table, lost; reported by later authors
milestones.description: Greek astronomers tabulate full chords of arcs; the Indian step is to switch to half-chords, i.e. the sine.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Trigonometric functions: first known table of chords by Hipparchus about 140 BC
Wikipedia, Aryabhata sine table: earlier tables by Hipparchus, Menelaus and Ptolemy were chord tables, not half-chord
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Aryabhata sine table (Aryabhata sine table redirect)

milestones.label: Siddhanta texts (incl. Surya Siddhanta) define sine as half-chord
milestones.work: Siddhantas, 4th-5th century; extant Surya Siddhanta probably revised c. 800
milestones.description: Astronomical treatises are credited with first defining sine as half of the chord of double the arc, but dating of surviving texts is uncertain.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia History of trigonometry: Siddhantas of the 4th-5th century first defined the sine as the half-chord relation
Wikipedia Surya Siddhanta: text dated end of 4th-5th century by most scholars; extant version composed or revised c. 800

milestones.note: Marked precursor because the surviving text is later than Aryabhata and unpublished earlier layers cannot be dated.

milestones.label: Aryabhata gives the first sine table (sine differences)
milestones.work: Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya, Dasagitika verse 12, 499
milestones.description: Aryabhata tabulates the sine differences of 24 arcs of 3 degrees 45 minutes with radius 3438, the earliest surviving table of half-chords.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Aryabhata: Aryabhatiya finished 499; table of sines at intervals of 90/24 degrees
Wikipedia Aryabhata sine table: first table of sines, first differences, radius 3438, verse 12 of Dasagitika
MacTutor Trigonometric functions: first actual appearance of the sine in the Hindu work, Aryabhata about 500, jya

milestones.label: Brahmagupta interpolates sine values with a second-order formula
milestones.work: Brahmagupta, Khandakhadyaka, 665 (also reproduces the table in 628)
milestones.description: Brahmagupta uses a second-order difference formula to compute sines between tabulated values; the same table appears in his 628 work.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Brahmagupta: in 665 devised second-order interpolation to find new sine values from tabulated ones
MacTutor Trigonometric functions: the table reproduced in the work of Brahmagupta in 628

milestones.label: Bhaskara II gives detailed methods to construct sine tables for any angle
milestones.work: Bhaskara II, Siddhantasiromani, 1150
milestones.description: Bhaskara gives detailed methods for constructing a sine table for any angle, extending earlier Indian tables.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Trigonometric functions: detailed method for constructing a table of sines for any angle given by Bhaskara in 1150

milestones.note: MacTutor assigns 1150 as a date for Bhaskara II works.

milestones.label: Fibonacci uses sinus rectus arcus; Latin sinus replaces Arabic jiba from jya
milestones.work: Fibonacci, Liber Abaci / Practica geometriae; translations of Arabic mathematics
milestones.description: Indian jya became Arabic jiba then jaib and was rendered Latin sinus; Fibonacci use of sinus rectus arcus helped fix the term.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Trigonometric functions: jya adopted by Arabs as jiba, then jaib, translated sinus; Fibonacci sinus rectus arcus encouraged universal use
Wikipedia History of trigonometry (etymology of sine via jya-ardha, jiva, jiba, sinus)

milestones.note: Earliest Latin use of sinus is by 12th-century translators; exact first use and year not established here (Fibonacci year 1202 is the Liber Abaci date, not verified for the specific passage).

milestones.label: Madhava of Sangamagrama gives power series for sine and refined sine tables
milestones.work: Madhava, c. 1350-1425
milestones.description: Continued attempts to improve the Aryabhata table culminated in series expansions and a seven- or eight-digit sine table.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Aryabhata sine table: improvements culminated in series for sine and cosine by Madhava (c. 1350-c. 1425)

milestones.note: Madhava works are known from later quotations; dating by his lifespan.

works.whyItMatters: Greek chord table that the sine replaces

notes: Disputed: whether the Aryabhata table adapts Greek chords (Wikipedia says the argument was refuted); date of the Siddhantas; Surya Siddhanta dating. Methodological date left null: the first purposeful use on planetary computation is inside Aryabhatiya and Siddhantas. Institutional date is the Latin naming and should be read as low confidence. Hipparchus biography URL not checked for 200 status (MacTutor).

milestones.label: Brahmi numerals appear
milestones.work: Ashokan inscriptions and Brahmi numerals, c. 3rd century BC
milestones.description: Additive Brahmi numeral signs for 1-9 and for tens and hundreds exist; they are not yet a place-value system.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Indian numerals: Brahmi numerals came into being around the middle of the third century BC; not place-value
Wikipedia Hindu-Arabic numeral system: Brahmi numerals predate the Common Era, on Ashoka edicts, and were not positional

milestones.label: Lokavibhaga: Jain cosmology text using decimal place value and zero
milestones.work: Lokavibhaga, internally dated 458 CE; surviving in a later Sanskrit translation
milestones.description: A Jain cosmological text, dated within itself to 458, may preserve one of the earliest positional uses of zero.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia, 0: Lokavibhaga internally dated to AD 458 uses decimal place value, including a zero; survives in later Sanskrit translation
Wikipedia Hindu-Arabic numeral system: Sanskrit translation of the lost 5th century Prakrit text may preserve an early instance

milestones.note: Only a later translation survives, so the date is inherited and may be revised; hence precursor not first_statement.

milestones.label: Aryabhatiya states the place-value principle
milestones.work: Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya, 499
milestones.description: Aryabhata states that each place is ten times the previous one and uses a word meaning emptiness for the empty position.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia 0: Aryabhatiya (499) states each place ten times the preceding
MacTutor Zero: around 500 Aryabhata devised a positional number system with no zero symbol; word kha for place
MacTutor Aryabhata: Aryabhatiya finished 499

milestones.note: The Aryabhatiya has a place-value statement but its own numerals are word-based and lack a zero symbol; first_statement of the idea in a securely dated text.

milestones.label: Earliest dated place-value document: Sankheda copper-plate charter
milestones.work: Donation charter of Dadda III of Sankheda, dated 346 in the Chhedi era (594 CE)
milestones.description: A dated charter writes a date in decimal place-value form, the oldest dated Indian document in that form according to MacTutor.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Indian numerals: oldest dated Indian document with place-value numbers is a charter dated Chhedi 346 = 594 AD

milestones.note: MacTutor itself flags a problem with the document (not detailed); treat with caution.

milestones.label: Brahmagupta states arithmetic rules for zero and negatives
milestones.work: Brahmagupta, Brahmasphutasiddhanta, 628
milestones.description: Brahmagupta defines zero as a number and sets sum, product and division rules, including a wrong rule for 0/0.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Brahmagupta: defines zero as a number minus itself and gives rules; attempts division by zero
Wikipedia, 0: rules for zero in Brahmasphuta Siddhanta (7th century)
Wikipedia Brahmagupta: Brahmasphutasiddhanta dated 628

milestones.label: Bakhshali manuscript (zero as a dot); date disputed
milestones.work: Bakhshali manuscript, birch bark, Gandhara region
milestones.description: The manuscript uses place value with a dot for zero, but its folios were radiocarbon dated across centuries.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Bakhshali manuscript: 2017 dates 224-383, 680-779, 885-993 CE; October 2024 revision 799-1102 CE; was regarded as earliest zero symbol until Sept 2024
Hayashi 1995, The Bakhshali Manuscript (Brill) records the study of the text

milestones.note: Do not rank by date: the manuscript contains layers and the 2017 and 2024 results disagree.

milestones.label: Gwalior inscription: first undisputed dated zero symbol
milestones.work: Chaturbhuj Temple inscription, Gwalior, dated 876 CE
milestones.description: A stone inscription writes 270 and 50 with a small circle for zero, the first dated writing of zero accepted as genuine.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Zero: first dated, agreed-genuine record of zero is the Gwalior inscription of 876
Wikipedia 0: first indubitable dated zero glyph in the Gwalior inscription AD 876; Khmer inscription of 683 mentioned

milestones.note: Cambodian Sambor inscription 605 Saka (683 CE) is mentioned in Wikipedia and dispute is flagged there.

works.whyItMatters: place-value statement and kha for empty place
proposes infinite quantity for division by zero

notes: Disputed: Bakhshali date (2017 vs October 2024 radiocarbon); Lokavibhaga date; Chinese or Babylonian origin theories for place value (MacTutor Indian numerals). No naming milestone dated (word sunya in Jain texts is claimed by Wikipedia Indian mathematics without a date). Institutional date null: no textbook/journal/code found in sources read. Event summary says "schools around 500-650"; sources support 499-628.

canonicalName: Interpolation and finite differences in Chinese astronomy and mathematics
aliases: Jade Mirror of the Four Unknowns

milestones.label: Liu Zhuo introduces second-order interpolation for calendar computation
milestones.work: Liu Zhuo, Huangji calendar (Sui dynasty); lifespan 544-610
milestones.description: Liu Zhuo uses second-order equal-interval differences to interpolate the sun irregular motion in the calendar.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Chinese overview: Liu Zhuo (544-610) introduced quadratic interpolation with second order difference
Ji Zhigang 1995 reconstructs Liu Zhuo second-order equal-interval interpolation (zbMATH)
evidence.source: Ji Zhigang, J. Northwest Univ. (1995), zbMATH 883363

evidence.claim: Ji Zhigang, From Liu Zhuo to Hua Hengfang (2002)
evidence.source: Historical Perspectives on East Asian Sciences, Tech. and Medicine

milestones.note: The calendar is usually dated about 600, but no date was found in the sources read; year given is the birth year of Liu Zhuo and the end year his death, so the range is a bound only. Derived conceptual date should be read as 6th-7th century.

milestones.label: Brahmagupta second-order interpolation of sines (parallel Indian tradition)
milestones.work: Brahmagupta, Khandakhadyaka, 665
milestones.description: An independent Indian formula equivalent to second-order interpolation used for sine tables; not a source for the Chinese work.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Brahmagupta: in 665 devised special case of second-order Newton-Stirling interpolation to find sine values

milestones.note: Included for comparison; influence between traditions is not claimed.

milestones.label: Guo Shoujing: cubic interpolation with tabulated differences in the Shoushi calendar
milestones.work: Guo Shoujing, Shoushi (Works and Days) calendar, completed 1280
milestones.description: Guo tabulates first, second and third differences of the accumulated difference, a third-order scheme resembling Newton forward differences.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Guo Shoujing: calendar completed by 1280; cubic interpolation formula with tabulated first, second and third differences
Ji Zhigang 1995 (zbMATH 883363): no breakthrough until Guo third-order method in 13th century

milestones.label: Zhu Shijie uses finite differences to sum series
milestones.work: Zhu Shijie, Siyuan yujian (Jade Mirror of the Four Unknowns), 1303
milestones.description: Zhu uses second, third and fourth differences to sum polynomial-type series such as the recruiting problem, moving the technique from astronomy to pure mathematics.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Zhu Shijie: Siyuan yujian 1303; solves recruiting-cubes problem by working out second, third, fourth differences
Wikipedia Zhu Shijie: Jade Mirror 1303 contains series and progressions classified via Pascal triangle coefficients
Chemla, Siyuan yujian entry in Encyclopaedia of the History of Science (2008)

works.whyItMatters: finite differences for sums of series

notes: The event is a transfer: a calendar tool applied to series by Zhu Shijie. Wikipedia Chinese mathematics also mentions He Chengtian (5th c.) fraction interpolation for pi; this is a different method (interpolating fractions) and was not made a milestone. Yi Xing (8th c.) and Tang calendar refinements are mentioned by Ji Zhigang (zbMATH review) but not dated here. No institution milestone: the field is far older than MSC. Conceptual derived date 544 is a lower bound only; the sources read give no year for the Huangji calendar.

canonicalName: Pell's equation and the chakravala method

milestones.label: Side and diagonal numbers: approximations to the square root of 2 in Greece and India
milestones.work: Pythagorean side/diagonal numbers; Baudhayana approximations 17/12, 577/408
milestones.description: Solutions of the N = 2 case of the equation give successive rational approximations of the square root of 2, known by about 400 BC.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Pell equation: as early as 400 BC in India and Greece mathematicians studied the N=2 case

milestones.label: Diophantus considers equations equivalent to Pell-type problems
milestones.work: Diophantus, Arithmetica
milestones.description: Diophantus solves problems of the form a x^2 + c = y^2 for several small cases, equivalent to Pell-type equations.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Pell equation: around AD 250 Diophantus considered equivalent equation for (a,c) = (1,1), (1,-1), (1,12), (3,9)
MacTutor Pell: Diophantus examines problems related to Pell equation

milestones.label: Brahmagupta composition (bhavana/samasa): generating solutions of x^2 - N y^2 = k
milestones.work: Brahmagupta, Brahmasphutasiddhanta, chapter 18, 628
milestones.description: Brahmagupta proves an identity composing two solutions into a third, so that one solution yields infinitely many, and solves cases such as N = 92 (1151, 120).

evidence.claim: MacTutor Pell: Brahmagupta lemma discovered in 628, method of composition, first to study the equation
Wikipedia Pell equation: Brahmagupta identity, composes triples, solved N = 92 with (1151, 120)
Colebrooke 1817 translation of Brahmagupta and Bhaskara (Algebra, with Arithmetic and Mensuration); Open Library

milestones.note: Verified (1151^2 - 92*120^2 = 1) by direct computation.

milestones.label: Jayadeva: general cyclic method
milestones.work: Jayadeva, c. 950-1000 (quoted in later works); Selenius analysis 1975
milestones.description: Jayadeva shows how to generalise Brahmagupta approach into the cyclic (chakravala) method.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Chakravala method: Jayadeva (c. 950-1000) pointed out that Brahmagupta approach could be generalised
Selenius 1975, Rationale of the chakravala process of Jayadeva and Bhaskara II

milestones.note: Jayadeva dates are approximate; some authors attribute the method to Bhaskara II (Wikipedia).

milestones.label: Bhaskara II: chakravala solves N = 61 (x = 226153980, y = 1766319049)
milestones.work: Bhaskara II, Bijaganita, 1150
milestones.description: Bhaskara II gives the cyclic algorithm that always terminates in a solution, and applies it to N = 61 where the smallest solution is huge.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Pell: Bhaskara II in 1150 discovered the cyclic method (chakravala)
MacTutor Bhaskara II: studied p = 8, 11, 32, 61, 67; gives x = 226153980 for 61
Wikipedia Pell equation: first general method for all N given by Bhaskara II in 1150; used for N = 61

milestones.note: MacTutor Bhaskara II page prints y as 1776319049, a typo; 61*226153980^2+1 equals 1766319049^2 (checked by computation).

milestones.label: Fermat's challenge; Brouncker and Wallis solve it (Commercium epistolicum 1658)
milestones.work: Fermat 1657 challenge; Wallis, Commercium epistolicum, 1658
milestones.description: Fermat challenges English mathematicians, and Brouncker finds a method close to continued fractions; Wallis publishes the exchange in 1658.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Pell: European interest began with Fermat challenge of 1657; Wallis published exchange in 1658
Open Library lists Commercium epistolicum (Brouncker and Wallis), 1658

milestones.label: Lagrange proves infinitely many solutions and systematises the continued-fraction method
milestones.work: Lagrange, work of 1766-1769; Additions to Euler Elements of Algebra, 1771
milestones.description: Lagrange gives a rigorous proof that the equation always has infinitely many solutions via continued fractions.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Pell: Euler continued-fraction approach polished by Lagrange in 1766; Additions 1771 proves infinitely many solutions
Wikipedia Pell equation: general theory developed by Lagrange in 1766-1769

milestones.note: Exact publication venues of the Lagrange memoirs were not verified.

milestones.label: Euler names it after Pell (misattribution)
milestones.work: Euler, naming of the equation
milestones.description: Euler, confusing Brouncker with Pell, gave the equation the name it still carries in the West.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Pell: Euler named it Pell equation, probably by confusing Brouncker and Pell
Wikipedia Pell equation: Pell revised the translation of Rahn Teutsche Algebra (1659); Euler named it after him by mistake

milestones.note: Year not established: searched MacTutor Pell and Wikipedia Pell; neither gives a year. Probably 18th century; do not rank.

works.whyItMatters: general chakravala algorithm and N = 61 solution

notes: Disputed: Brahmagupta versus Bhaskara II versus Jayadeva for the first general method; Brahmagupta method is not general for all N. Dates of Euler naming not found. Hankel quotation of chakravala as best before Lagrange appears on Wikipedia; not needed as a milestone. MSC 11D09 (quadratic and bilinear equations) exists but its first year was not established. Lifespans for Brouncker are from memory and flagged. Methodological date left null: first purposeful application of the tool on a target is not separable from the first statement.

aliases: Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing

milestones.label: Old Babylonian algebraic procedures
milestones.work: Old Babylonian tablets
milestones.description: Quadratic-type problems were already solved by explicit procedures long before the Baghdad school.

evidence.claim: Hoyrup 2002 chapters on Old Babylonian algebra

milestones.note: Date is the conventional Old Babylonian period (c. 1800-1600 BCE) and not given in the chapter metadata.

milestones.label: Diophantus: algebraic solution with symbolic abbreviations
milestones.work: Diophantus, Arithmetica
milestones.description: Arithmetica solves numerical problems with a named unknown and simplification to standard form, a Greek precursor concerned with number theory.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Arithmetica (in Diophantus): three-stage method like medieval Arabic algebra; no classification into six types

milestones.note: Cross-reference to event on Diophantus.

milestones.label: Brahmagupta: first clear quadratic formula in Brahmasphutasiddhanta
milestones.work: Brahmagupta, Brahmasphutasiddhanta, 628
milestones.description: An Indian text gives rules for quadratic equations a century before al-Jabr, in verse and with negative numbers.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Brahmagupta: first clear description of quadratic formula; Brahmasphutasiddhanta dated 628
Wikipedia Al-Jabr: Islamic mathematicians unlike Hindus did not treat negative numbers

milestones.label: Al-Jabr: first book to teach algebra for its own sake
milestones.work: Al-Khwarizmi, Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wa al-muqabala, Baghdad c. 820
milestones.description: Al-Khwarizmi classifies equations into six normal forms with their solutions and geometric proofs, treating algebra as an independent subject.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Al-Jabr: written in Baghdad around 820; first text to teach elementary algebra for its own sake; six types of quadratic equations
MacTutor Al-Khwarizmi: algebra treatise in Baghdad (born about 780, died about 850)
Gandz 1936 on the sources of al-Khwarizmi algebra (Osiris)

milestones.note: Katz dates it around 825 (quoted on Wikipedia).

milestones.label: Title gives the word algebra
milestones.work: Al-Jabr; Latin Liber algebrae et almucabala
milestones.description: The Arabic term al-jabr in the title, restoring a subtracted term to the other side, is the origin of the word algebra.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Al-Jabr: title is the ultimate etymology of the word algebra; al-jabr and al-muqabala defined
Gandz 1926, The origin of the term algebra (Amer. Math. Monthly)

milestones.note: The same work plays first_statement and naming; kept separate because they are different facts (the book versus the term).

milestones.label: Robert of Chester translates Al-Jabr into Latin
milestones.work: Robert of Chester, Liber algebrae, 1145
milestones.description: The Latin translation makes algebra the standard university text in Europe until the sixteenth century.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Al-Jabr: translated into Latin by Robert of Chester in 1145; principal textbook until the sixteenth century
Wikipedia Al-Khwarizmi: Al-Jabr translated by Robert of Chester in 1145

works.whyItMatters: first textbook of algebra as a subject

notes: Disputed: whether al-Khwarizmi is more entitled to be called father of algebra than Diophantus (Wikipedia notes the claim). The original Arabic title and date are approximate (around 820-825). Methodological date left null: first purposeful application (inheritance and legal problems in the book itself, see Gandz 1938 doi 10.1086/368492) is in the same work. Abu Kamil dating: lifespans from MacTutor are about 850-930.

canonicalName: Transmission of Hindu-Arabic numerals to the Islamic world and Europe

milestones.label: Indian place-value reckoning taken up in Islamic mathematics
milestones.work: 8th century, recorded later by al-Qifti
milestones.description: Indian developments reach Islamic scholars in the 8th century according to a 13th-century chronicle.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Hindu-Arabic numeral system: taken up in Islamic mathematics in the 8th century as recorded by al-Qifti

milestones.note: Single secondary source; centuries later chronicle.

milestones.label: Al-Khwarizmi writes on calculation with Hindu numerals
milestones.work: Al-Khwarizmi, On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals, c. 825; Arabic text lost, Latin Algoritmi de numero Indorum
milestones.description: The book explains the Indian decimal place-value method in Arabic; it is credited as chiefly responsible for spreading it in the Middle East and Europe.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Al-Khwarizmi: On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals written about 825, spread the system; Latin Algoritmi de numero Indorum
Wikipedia Hindu-Arabic numeral system: Khwarizmi, about 825 CE

milestones.note: Arabic original not extant; the work is known through Latin versions. Date approximate.

milestones.label: Al-Kindi writes on the use of the Hindu numerals
milestones.work: Al-Kindi, On the Use of the Hindu Numerals, c. 830
milestones.description: A second early Arabic treatise on the Indian numerals appears about the same time.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Hindu-Arabic numeral system: Al-Kindi book around 830 CE
MacTutor lists Al-Kindi (born about 801, died 873)

milestones.label: Al-Uqlidisi: earliest extant Arabic arithmetic, with decimal fractions
milestones.work: Al-Uqlidisi, Kitab al-fusul fi al-hisab al-hindi, Damascus 952-53; ed. Saidan
milestones.description: The earliest surviving Arabic arithmetic in the Indian system extends it to decimal fractions.

evidence.claim: MacTutor Al-Uqlidisi: composed text in Damascus in 952-53; place value, operations, decimal and sexagesimal
Saidan 1966, The earliest extant Arabic arithmetic: Kitab al-Fusul
Wikipedia Hindu-Arabic numeral system: first to describe positional decimal fractions

milestones.label: Latin Algoritmi: algorithm takes its name from al-Khwarizmi
milestones.work: 12th-century Latin translation of the Hindu reckoning treatise
milestones.description: The Latin version Algoritmi de numero Indorum gives the Western word algorithm and the term algorism for the new arithmetic.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Al-Khwarizmi: 12th-century Latin translation introduced the term algorithm to the West

milestones.note: 12th century as a range; translator and manuscript not checked.

milestones.label: Fibonacci Liber Abaci: the new numerals for Latin merchants
milestones.work: Fibonacci, Liber Abaci, 1202
milestones.description: Fibonacci presents the Indian method with applications to commerce, the major source for European adoption.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia Liber Abaci: 1202 Latin work introducing base-10 positional notation in Europe
Sigler translation of Liber Abaci (2002), Open Library
MacTutor Fibonacci biography

works.citation: On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals
On the Use of the Hindu Numerals

notes: The event sits between event P111 (origin of place value) and the European story. The question of Chinese influence on Sunzi division (Wikipedia Chinese mathematics) is not used. Other Arabic works (Kushyar, Abu Kamil) not dated. Naming is low confidence: the term algorism appears after translation. Institutional derived date 1100 is the start of the range and needs attention.
